scarcity-s1.title: One empty lot in Riverton
scarcity-s1.html: The town of Riverton (an invented town) owns one empty lot downtown. Residents want a park, store owners want a parking garage, and a grocery chain offers to lease the lot for a new store. Building the garage would take a crew of 40 construction workers, two cranes and a fleet of dump trucks, and a local developer has offered to put up her own savings to run the project.

items.q: What makes the choice about Riverton's lot an economic problem?
options: The town has run out of money for any project
The lot cannot be used for a park, a garage and a store at the same time
Store owners care more than residents do
The grocery chain sets the price of the lease

items.q: Which factor of production is the lot itself?
options: Land
Labor
Capital
Entrepreneurship

items.q: In the garage plan, which item is capital?
options: The 40 construction workers
The empty lot
The developer's willingness to risk her savings
The two cranes and the dump trucks

items.q: The developer offers her own savings to run the garage project. Which factor of production does she supply, and why?
options: Capital, because she provides money
Labor, because she works on the project
Entrepreneurship, because she organizes the project and takes the risk
Land, because the garage sits on the lot

items.q: Which country in the table has a command economy?
options: Lorna
Pavlo
Quill
Lorna and Quill together

items.q: Which country in the table is closest to how most real economies work?
options: Quill, a mixed economy
Lorna, a pure market economy
Pavlo, a pure command economy
Pavlo and Lorna equally

items.q: In Lorna, how is the "for whom" question mostly answered?
options: By government planners assigning goods to each household
By giving each household the same amount
By the order in which people line up
By who is willing and able to pay market prices

items.q: In Pavlo, a factory manager is told to make 500 tractors this year. Which basic question has the government answered?
options: For whom to produce
Whether resources are scarce
What to produce
How much to charge buyers

items.q: Which statement about scarcity is accurate?
options: It ends once a country becomes rich enough
It exists because wants are greater than the resources to meet them
It applies to goods but not to time
It means a store has sold out of a product

items.q: A student has three free hours on Saturday and wants to study, work a paid shift and see friends. What does this show?
options: Scarcity: limited time forces a choice among wants
An economic system answering the question of for whom to produce
A command decision by the student's parents
A factor of production called entrepreneurship

items.q: A city council spends this year's budget on a new bridge, so it repairs fewer school buildings. What is this an example of?
options: A command economy
An increase in resources
A choice with nothing given up
A trade-off

items.q: Which of these are capital in the economic sense? Select all that apply.
options: A delivery van owned by a bakery
A robot arm on a car assembly line
Cash a bakery keeps in its bank account
Crude oil still in the ground

items.q: Which is a service rather than a good?
options: A pair of scissors
A bottle of shampoo
A haircut
A barber's chair

items.q: A country discovers a large new field of natural gas. Which factor of production has it gained more of?
options: Labor
Land
Capital
Entrepreneurship

items.q: A neighbor says, "Scarcity is not a problem for billionaires." What is the best reply?
options: They still face limited time and must choose how to use it and their money
They are right: with enough money each want is met
They are right, at least in a market economy
Scarcity applies to governments, not to people

items.q: Put the steps from scarcity to a decision in order.
options: Wants are greater than the resources available
Resources are scarce
People must choose how to use them
Each choice gives up something else (a trade-off)

items.q: Label this production possibilities curve for an economy that makes pizzas (on the horizontal axis) and robots (on the vertical axis).
A recession leaves many factories idle and many workers without jobs. Place point U to show what the economy produces.
Place point Z at a combination of pizzas and robots the economy cannot produce with its current resources and technology.
Every worker and machine is employed in its best use. Place point F to show one combination the economy could produce.
A new technology raises how much of both goods the economy can make. Show the change on the graph.

key.because: a new technology that raises output of both goods

items.q: A hurricane destroys many factories and farms. Show the change on the graph.

key.because: a hurricane that destroys factories and farms

items.q: Using the table, what is the opportunity cost per million bushels of wheat when Arland moves from combination 2 to combination 3?

mistakes.why: You divided the wheat gained by the tractors given up. Opportunity cost is what is given up per unit gained: 4 / 10.
That is the total cost of the 10 million bushels. The question asks per million bushels: divide by 10.

items.q: Using the table, how many thousand tractors does Arland give up in total to move from combination 3 to combination 4?

mistakes.why: That is the number of tractors still made at combination 4. The cost is how many were given up: 14 - 8.
That is the wheat gained. The opportunity cost is measured in the good given up, tractors.

items.q: What does the table show about Arland's opportunity cost of wheat as it makes more wheat?
options: It stays the same: each extra 10 million bushels costs 2 thousand tractors
It rises: each extra 10 million bushels costs more tractors than the last
It falls: wheat gets cheaper to make as Arland makes more
It is impossible to find from a table

items.q: Could Arland produce 25 million bushels of wheat and 14 thousand tractors in the same year?
options: No: that combination lies outside its PPC
Yes: it lies inside its PPC, with resources to spare
Yes: it lies on its PPC
Yes, once it gives up some wheat

items.q: Arland is producing 20 million bushels of wheat and 10 thousand tractors. What does this tell you?
options: It is producing at an efficient point
It has the best technology in the world
It has just lost a large share of its factories in a hurricane
Some of its resources are unemployed or used inefficiently

items.q: What change could explain the move from the faded curve to the new one in the graph?
options: Bellmark puts its idle factories back to work
The price of machines rises
Bellmark gains more workers and better machines
Bellmark shifts workers from making food to making machines

items.q: A combination of food and machines lay just outside Bellmark's faded curve. Where does it lie now?
options: It is still unattainable, because the whole curve shifted
It may now be attainable, on or inside the new curve
It is now inside the faded curve
It has moved to the horizontal axis

items.q: Bellmark's new curve still bows outward. What does that shape tell you?
options: Resources are not equally good at making food and machines
Each extra unit of food costs the same number of machines
Bellmark has idle resources
Bellmark is unable to make more of both goods

items.q: Jordan's Saturday options, in order of preference, are a hike with friends, a paid work shift worth $80, and studying. If Jordan goes on the hike, what is the opportunity cost?
options: The work shift and the studying, added together
Nothing, because the hike is free
The studying, because it ranks last
The $80 work shift, the next-best choice

items.q: A country's PPC is a straight line from 60 thousand shirts (and no jackets) to 20 thousand jackets (and no shirts). What is the opportunity cost of one jacket, in shirts?

mistakes.why: That is the cost of one shirt in jackets (20 / 60). For a jacket, divide the shirts given up by the jackets gained: 60 / 20.

items.q: An economy spends more of its resources this year on factories and machines and less on consumer goods. What happens to its PPC in the future?
options: It shifts in, because people have fewer consumer goods today
It stays where it is, because total resources are unchanged
It shifts out farther, because the extra capital raises future production
It becomes a straight line

items.q: Why is a production possibilities curve usually bowed outward rather than straight?
options: Each resource is equally good at making both goods
Some resources are better at making one good than the other
The economy has idle resources at each point
Prices rise as output rises

items.q: Using the table, what is Corvia's opportunity cost of making one hat, in shirts?

mistakes.why: That is the cost of one shirt in hats (8 / 24). For one hat, divide the shirts given up by the hats gained: 24 / 8.

items.q: Which country has the absolute advantage in hats?
options: Delmont, because it has the lower opportunity cost of making hats
Corvia, because one worker makes 8 hats a day to Delmont's 6
Delmont, because it makes fewer shirts per worker
Neither, because both countries make hats

items.q: Which country has the comparative advantage in hats?
options: Delmont, because a hat costs it 2 shirts and costs Corvia 3
Corvia, because each of its workers makes more hats per day
Corvia, because it makes more of both goods
Delmont, because it makes fewer shirts

items.q: If both countries specialize by comparative advantage, what does each produce?
options: Corvia makes both, because it is better at both
Corvia makes hats and Delmont makes shirts
Each makes half of each good
Corvia makes shirts and Delmont makes hats

items.q: Which terms of trade would benefit both countries?
options: 1 hat for 1.5 shirts
1 hat for 3.5 shirts
1 hat for 2.5 shirts
1 hat for 4 shirts

items.q: Using the table, what is Fenwick's opportunity cost of making one table, in chairs?

mistakes.why: You inverted it, as you would with output data. With hours per unit, a table costs (hours per table) / (hours per chair) = 6 / 2 chairs.

items.q: Which country has the absolute advantage in chairs?
options: Fenwick, because it needs more hours per chair
Ellis, because it needs 1 hour per chair to Fenwick's 2
Fenwick, because it has the lower opportunity cost of chairs
Neither, because both need hours to make chairs

items.q: Which country has the comparative advantage in chairs?
options: Fenwick, because a chair costs it a third of a table and costs Ellis half a table
Ellis, because it needs fewer hours per chair
Ellis, because it is faster at both goods
Fenwick, because it needs more hours per table

items.q: A student says, "Ellis needs fewer hours for both goods, so trade with Fenwick cannot help Ellis." What is wrong with the claim?
options: Nothing: a country with the absolute advantage in both goods gains nothing from trading with others
Ellis gains if Fenwick also has an absolute advantage in something
Trade helps Ellis if it switches to making chairs
Ellis gains by making tables and buying chairs at a price below its own opportunity cost

items.q: A surgeon types faster than her assistant but pays the assistant to do her typing. Which idea explains this?
options: Absolute advantage: the assistant types faster than the surgeon
Scarcity: there is not enough typing to go around
Comparative advantage: an hour of typing costs the surgeon far more surgery than it costs the assistant
Increasing opportunity cost: typing gets harder the more she does

items.q: Can one country have the comparative advantage in both of two goods?
options: Yes: if it has the absolute advantage in both
No: if its opportunity cost of one good is lower, its opportunity cost of the other is higher
Yes: if it has more workers
Yes: if its PPC is farther out

items.q: Two countries specialize by comparative advantage and trade at terms between their opportunity costs. Which results follow? Select all that apply.
options: Their combined output of the two goods can rise
Each can consume a combination outside its own PPC
The country with the absolute advantage in both goods gains and the other loses
Each country's PPC shifts outward

items.q: Two countries have the same opportunity cost of wheat in terms of cloth. What does this imply about trade between them?
options: Neither gains from specializing and trading these goods
Both gain a great deal
The larger country gains and the smaller loses
They gain as long as the terms of trade are set high enough

items.q: Why must mutually beneficial terms of trade lie between the two countries' opportunity costs?
options: The richer country sets the price
Prices in trade are set at the exact average of the two costs
Countries trade goods they are unable to make
Each country must get a good for less than it costs to make at home

items.q: In Corvia one worker makes 24 shirts or 8 hats a day. Corvia trades for hats at 1 hat for 2.5 shirts. How many shirts does Corvia save on each hat it buys instead of making it?

mistakes.why: That is the price Corvia pays. The gain is its own opportunity cost (3 shirts) minus that price.
That is what a hat costs Corvia to make. The gain is that cost minus the 2.5 shirts it pays.

items.q: Put the steps for finding comparative advantage from an output table in order.
options: Find each country's opportunity cost of each good
Compare the two countries' opportunity costs for each good
Give each good to the country with its lower opportunity cost
Choose terms of trade between the two opportunity costs
